extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and scientifically literate readers (readers of Popular Science Monthly) and professional scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for critiquing physical theories and scientific reviews: assessing conceptual clarity, empirical fit, parsimony, and the conduct of reviewers. Focuses on how to judge a scientific theory and how reviewers should argue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scientific terms according to exact definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of using scientific terms only in accordance with their exact definitions; of ascertaining the meanings of the words mass and motion by a reference to the methods whereby they are measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting the page: reviewers should determine term meanings by reference to how they are measured. Example given: Newcomb's criticism that the author used 'mass' as a concrete term whereas it is an 'abstract noun' — the page argues one must be careful about such charges and see how terms function in the theory. Guidance: do not attack authors for terminology without checking context and the measurement-based sense of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing concepts with things (do not reify abstractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'great fundamental vice' of the mechanical theory is the confusion of concepts with things; beware hypostasizing or reifying abstractions (giving abstract nouns the status of concrete objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains reification: putting an abstract noun 'on a shelf' or personifying/deifying it. Anti-pattern: treating abstractions as tangible entities leads to conceptual error. Recommendation: keep concepts distinct from ontological claims about things.

rubrics_metrics.name: A valid physical theory must be a simplification (parsimony / reduction of independent variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every valid physical theory is essentially a simplification and not a complication — a reduction of the number of unrelated facts which it undertakes to account for; in mathematical language, a reduction of the number of independent variables representing the phenomena to be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts genuine theory-building (explaining many phenomena by fewer independent assumptions) with the illegitimate substitution of many arbitrary, unverifiable assumptions for a few known facts. Use parsimony as a key evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory must accord with empirical facts and precise observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories collapse in the presence of facts; a theory implying effects inconsistent with precise observational data (e.g., planetary orbital timing) is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cooke's argument about a luminiferous ether imposing resistance on Earth's motion — astronomical precision would detect such drag, so an ether with large resistance is untenable. Guidance: check quantitative observational consequences of theoretical assumptions against high-precision data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer theories that explain diverse phenomena using best-known properties (explanatory power)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good theory 'explains with the utmost simplicity ... a great number of diverse phenomena, seemingly incapable of explanation in any other way', using only the best-known properties of entities invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Professor Newcomb's praise of the kinetic theory: explanatory breadth using well-established properties is a virtue. Evaluate theories on how many independent phenomena they unify and whether they rely on well-established properties rather than ad hoc assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should present concrete abstracts or refutations rather than dismiss as 'impossible'
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that merely asserts 'an abstract is impossible' or dismisses objections without summarizing them is inadequate; reviewers ought to attempt to abstract and, if possible, refute the objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author objects to Newcomb's remark that 'an abstract of them is impossible' and urges that making an abstract of objections does not appear difficult. Practice guidance: when criticizing a work, provide clear summaries of the opposing arguments and explicit refutations instead of rhetorical dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scientific dogmatism; maintain openness and candid investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists should avoid treating dominant theories as sacred and violently repelling attempts to point out defects; a candid investigator should examine difficulties rather than dogmatically defend theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts dogmatic defenders of dominant theories with honest investigators like Maxwell who recognized difficulties. Recommendation: foster humility, entertain critiques, and consider consequences rather than reflexive defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for internal degrees of freedom and energy exchanges in physical models
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical model must consider internal vibrations/degrees of freedom and their effect on observable quantities (e.g., specific heat); assumptions that remove or ignore such internal modes can lead to incorrect predictions (e.g., infinite specific heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawn from the Maxwell/Boltzmann discussion: constructing 'rigid-elastic' bodies or assuming atoms without internal modes can produce paradoxes (infinite degrees of freedom or incorrect energy partition). Guidance: evaluate whether a theory correctly treats internal degrees of freedom and energy exchange (with ether or radiation) and respects conservation/partition results.
